levels.title: A1 · Principiante
levels.description: Te presentas, hablas de ti, tu familia y tu rutina con frases sencillas.

units.title: Hola, soy…
units.subtitle: Saludos y el verbo to be (I am / you are)
units.goal: Saludar, presentarte y decir de dónde eres.

sections.heading: El verbo to be
sections.body:
**To be** significa *ser* o *estar*. En presente tiene tres formas:

- I **am** (yo soy/estoy)
- you / we / they **are**
- he / she / it **is**

En conversación casi siempre se usan contracciones: **I'm**, **you're**, **he's**, **she's**, **it's**, **we're**, **they're**.

> I'm Denil. I'm from Guatemala.
> She's a teacher.
> We're students.

sections.heading: Saludos y despedidas
sections.body:
- **Hello / Hi** → hola (Hi es más informal)
- **Good morning / Good afternoon / Good evening** → buenos días / buenas tardes / buenas noches (al llegar)
- **Good night** → buenas noches (solo al despedirte o irte a dormir)
- **Nice to meet you** → mucho gusto
- **See you later / Bye** → nos vemos / adiós

Para preguntar el nombre: **What's your name?** → **My name is…** o **I'm…**
Para preguntar el origen: **Where are you from?** → **I'm from…**

sections.heading: Ojo: el sujeto siempre va
sections.body:
En español decimos *soy estudiante* sin "yo". En inglés **el sujeto es obligatorio**: no se dice *Am a student*, sino **I'm a student**.

Con profesiones se usa **a / an**: **I'm a developer**, **She's an engineer**.

examples.en: Hi! I'm Denil.
Nice to meet you.
Where are you from?
I'm from Guatemala.
She's a teacher.
We're friends.
They're in the classroom.
It's a beautiful city.

exercises.prompt: Son las 9 p. m. y llegas a una reunión. Dices:
exercises.explain: **Good night** es solo para despedirse; al llegar se dice **Good evening**.

units.title: ¿Eres…? No, no soy…
units.subtitle: To be: negativo, preguntas y números
units.goal: Hacer preguntas de sí/no, negar y usar números del 0 al 100.

sections.heading: Negativo
sections.body:
Se agrega **not** después de to be:

- I'm **not** tired.
- He **isn't** (is not) here.
- We **aren't** (are not) ready.

Ojo: no existe *amn't*. Con I se dice **I'm not**.

sections.heading: Preguntas
sections.body:
Se invierte el orden: el verbo va **antes** del sujeto.

> Are you a student? — Yes, I am. / No, I'm not.
> Is she your sister? — Yes, she is. / No, she isn't.

En respuestas cortas afirmativas **no** se usa contracción: *Yes, I am* (no *Yes, I'm*).

Preguntas con palabra interrogativa: **How old are you?** (¿cuántos años tienes?) → **I'm 20.** En inglés la edad se dice con *be*, no con *have*.

sections.heading: Números
sections.body:
- 1-12: one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve
- 13-19 terminan en **-teen**: thirteen, fourteen, fifteen…
- Decenas terminan en **-ty**: twenty, thirty, forty (¡sin u!), fifty…
- 21 = twenty-one, 99 = ninety-nine, 100 = one hundred

Cuidado al escuchar: **thirteen** (13) tiene el acento al final; **thirty** (30) al inicio.

examples.en: I'm not tired.
Are you ready?
Yes, I am.
Is he your brother?
No, he isn't. He's my cousin.
How old are you?
I'm twenty years old.
It isn't expensive.

exercises.prompt: She ___ at home. She's at work.

exercises.explain: En respuestas cortas afirmativas no se contrae: **Yes, I am.**
La edad se dice con **be**: I'm 25 (years old).

units.title: Cosas a mi alrededor
units.subtitle: Artículos, plurales y this/that/these/those
units.goal: Nombrar objetos, usar a/an/the y señalar cosas cerca o lejos.

sections.heading: A / an / the
sections.body:
- **a** antes de sonido de consonante: a book, a car, **a university** (suena "iu")
- **an** antes de sonido de vocal: an apple, an idea, **an hour** (la h no suena)
- **the** = el/la/los/las, cuando ya sabemos de cuál hablamos.

> I have a dog. The dog is black.

sections.heading: Plurales
sections.body:
- La mayoría: + **s** → book**s**, car**s**
- Terminados en s, sh, ch, x: + **es** → bus**es**, watch**es**, box**es**
- Consonante + y → **ies**: city → cit**ies** (pero day → day**s**)
- Irregulares: man → **men**, woman → **women**, child → **children**, person → **people**, foot → **feet**, tooth → **teeth**

Los adjetivos **no** cambian en plural: *two big houses* (no *bigs*).

sections.heading: This, that, these, those
sections.body:
- Cerca, singular: **this** (este/esta)
- Cerca, plural: **these** (estos/estas)
- Lejos, singular: **that** (ese/aquel)
- Lejos, plural: **those** (esos/aquellos)

> This is my phone. Those are my keys.

examples.en: This is my laptop.
Those cars are expensive.
I need an umbrella.
The children are in the park.
examples.es: Los niños están en el parque.

examples.en: These shoes are new.
That is a good idea.
There are three people here.
It's an old house.

vocab.ex: My phone is on the table.
The keys are on the table.

exercises.explain: apple empieza con sonido de vocal → **an**.

exercises.prompt: (Lejos, plural) ___ are my friends over there.
Los niños están en el parque.
answers: The children are in the park.

units.title: Mi familia
units.subtitle: Posesivos, 's y pronombres
units.goal: Hablar de tu familia y de quién es cada cosa.

sections.heading: Adjetivos posesivos
sections.body:
Van antes del sustantivo y **no** cambian en plural:

- I → **my** · you → **your** · he → **his** · she → **her**
- it → **its** · we → **our** · they → **their**

> My parents live in Ciudad Vieja. Their house is big.

Cuidado: **its** (de él/ella, cosa) ≠ **it's** (it is).

sections.heading: El 's para decir 'de'
sections.body:
En español: *el carro de mi papá*. En inglés: **my dad's car**.

- Singular: my sister**'s** room
- Plural con s: my parents**'** house (solo apóstrofo)
- Plural irregular: the children**'s** toys

sections.heading: La familia
sections.body:
- mother / father → **parents**
- son / daughter → **children**
- brother / sister → **siblings**
- grandmother / grandfather → **grandparents**
- uncle / aunt / cousin / nephew / niece
- husband / wife

Pregunta útil: **Do you have any brothers or sisters?**

examples.en: This is my family.
My mother's name is Rosa.
examples.es: El nombre de mi mamá es Rosa.

examples.en: Their house is in Antigua.
examples.es: Su casa (de ellos) está en Antigua.

examples.en: Her brother is a doctor.
examples.es: El hermano de ella es doctor.

examples.en: Our dog is very friendly.
My parents' car is red.
examples.es: El carro de mis papás es rojo.

examples.en: I have two cousins.
What's your sister's name?

vocab.ex: Their son is ten years old.
My uncle lives in the US.
My cousin is my best friend.

units.title: Mi día
units.subtitle: Presente simple: afirmativo y la hora
units.goal: Describir tu rutina diaria y decir la hora.

sections.heading: Presente simple
sections.body:
Se usa para **rutinas**, **hábitos** y **cosas que siempre son verdad**.

Con I / you / we / they el verbo va igual: **I work**, **they live**.

Con **he / she / it** se agrega **-s**: she work**s**, he live**s**.

- Terminados en s, sh, ch, x, o: + **es** → watch**es**, go**es**, do**es**
- Consonante + y: **-ies** → study → stud**ies**
- **have** → **has**

sections.heading: La hora
sections.body:
- **What time is it?** → **It's seven o'clock.** (7:00)
- 7:15 → **It's quarter past seven** / **It's seven fifteen**
- 7:30 → **It's half past seven** / **It's seven thirty**
- 7:45 → **It's quarter to eight** / **It's seven forty-five**

Preposición: **at** 7 o'clock · **in** the morning / afternoon / evening · **at** night

examples.en: I get up at six o'clock.
She works from home.
He studies at the university.
We have breakfast at seven.
My brother goes to the gym in the evening.
examples.es: Mi hermano va al gimnasio en la noche.

examples.en: The class starts at half past eight.
examples.es: La clase empieza a las ocho y media.

examples.en: I go to bed at eleven.
It's quarter to nine.

vocab.ex: I get up early on weekdays.
He takes a shower every morning.
I go to work by car.

exercises.prompt: I go to the gym ___ the evening.
My sister ___ (go) to school by bus.

answers: I get up at six o'clock.

exercises.prompt: Mi hermano va al gimnasio en la noche.
answers: My brother goes to the gym in the evening.

exercises.explain: He takes a shower every morning.

units.title: ¿Lo haces seguido?
units.subtitle: Presente simple: negativo, preguntas y frecuencia
units.goal: Preguntar y negar en presente y decir con qué frecuencia haces algo.

sections.heading: Negativo con don't / doesn't
sections.body:
- I / you / we / they → **don't** + verbo
- he / she / it → **doesn't** + verbo **sin -s**

> I don't like coffee.
> She doesn't work on Sundays. (no *doesn't works*)

sections.heading: Preguntas con do / does
sections.body:
> **Do** you speak English? — Yes, I do. / No, I don't.
> **Does** he play soccer? — Yes, he does. / No, he doesn't.
> Where **do** you live? · What time **does** the bank open?

Otra vez: con does el verbo va **sin -s**.

sections.heading: Adverbios de frecuencia
sections.body:
**always** (100%) → **usually** → **often** → **sometimes** → **rarely** → **never** (0%)

Van **antes** del verbo principal, pero **después** de to be:

> I **usually** walk to work.
> She is **always** late.

Pregunta: **How often do you…?** → once a week, twice a month, every day.

examples.en: I don't like coffee.
She doesn't eat meat.
Do you speak English?
Where does your brother live?
I usually take the bus.
He is never late.
How often do you exercise?
We go to the beach twice a year.
examples.es: Vamos a la playa dos veces al año.

vocab.ex: I drink a lot of water.
I call my mom once a week.

exercises.prompt: ___ often do you go to the cinema?

units.title: Mi casa
units.subtitle: There is / there are y preposiciones de lugar
units.goal: Describir tu casa y decir dónde están las cosas.

sections.heading: There is / there are
sections.body:
Significa **hay**:

- Singular: **There is (There's)** a sofa in the living room.
- Plural: **There are** two bedrooms.
- Negativo: **There isn't** a garage. / **There aren't** any chairs.
- Pregunta: **Is there** a bank near here? — Yes, there is.

sections.heading: Preposiciones de lugar
sections.body:
- **in** = dentro de → in the box, in the kitchen
- **on** = sobre (tocando) → on the table, on the wall
- **under** = debajo de
- **next to** = al lado de
- **between** = entre
- **in front of** = enfrente de · **behind** = detrás de
- **near** = cerca de

> The cat is under the bed.
> The bank is between the pharmacy and the school.

examples.es: Hay una ventana grande en mi cuarto.

units.title: Puedo hacerlo
units.subtitle: Can / can't y el imperativo
units.goal: Hablar de habilidades, pedir permiso y dar instrucciones.

sections.heading: Can / can't
sections.body:
**can** + verbo base = poder / saber hacer algo. Es igual para todas las personas (sin -s).

> I can swim. She can play the guitar.
> He **can't** (cannot) drive.
> **Can** you help me? — Yes, I can. / No, I can't.

También sirve para **pedir** algo o **permiso**: *Can I open the window?*

sections.heading: Imperativo
sections.body:
Para dar órdenes, instrucciones o consejos se usa el verbo base **sin sujeto**:

> Open your books. Turn left. Be careful!

Negativo con **Don't**: *Don't touch that. Don't be late.*

Para sonar amable agrega **please**: *Please sit down.*

examples.en: I can speak two languages.
She can't drive.
Can you help me, please?
Can I use your phone?
Open the window, please.
Don't be late.
Turn left at the corner.
examples.es: Gira a la izquierda en la esquina.

examples.en: He can cook very well.

units.title: ¿Qué estás haciendo?
units.subtitle: Presente continuo
units.goal: Describir lo que pasa en este momento.

sections.heading: Forma
sections.body:
**am / is / are** + verbo con **-ing**:

> I'm working. She's sleeping. They're playing.
> I'm **not** watching TV.
> **Are** you listening? — Yes, I am.

Ortografía del -ing:
- write → wri**ting** (se quita la e)
- run → ru**nning**, sit → si**tting** (consonante doble)
- lie → **lying**

sections.heading: Presente simple vs continuo
sections.body:
- **Simple**: rutinas → *I work every day.*
- **Continuo**: ahora mismo / temporal → *I'm working now.* · *I'm living with my cousin this month.*

Palabras típicas del continuo: **now**, **right now**, **at the moment**, **today**, **Look!**, **Listen!**

Algunos verbos casi nunca van en continuo: **like, love, want, need, know, understand**. Se dice *I want coffee*, no *I'm wanting*.

examples.en: I'm studying English right now.
She's talking on the phone.
Look! It's raining.
What are you doing?
They aren't listening.
We're watching a movie.
He's running in the park.
examples.es: Él está corriendo en el parque.

examples.en: I need help.

vocab.ex: She's at work at the moment.

answers: I am looking for my keys

units.title: En el súper
units.subtitle: Contables, incontables, some/any, much/many
units.goal: Hablar de comida, cantidades y hacer compras.

sections.heading: Contables e incontables
sections.body:
- **Contables**: se pueden contar → an apple, two apples
- **Incontables**: no tienen plural → water, rice, money, bread, information, advice

No se dice *a water* ni *breads*: se dice **some water**, **a bottle of water**, **a piece of bread**.

sections.heading: Some / any
sections.body:
- **some**: en afirmativas → *There's some milk.*
- **any**: en negativas y preguntas → *There isn't any sugar. Do you have any eggs?*
- Para ofrecer o pedir se usa **some** en preguntas: *Would you like some coffee?*

sections.heading: Much / many / a lot of
sections.body:
- **How many** + contable plural → *How many eggs do we need?*
- **How much** + incontable → *How much water do you drink?*
- **How much is it?** → ¿Cuánto cuesta?
- **a lot of** sirve para los dos en afirmativo: *a lot of friends, a lot of money*.

examples.en: Can I have some water, please?
There isn't any milk.
How many eggs do we need?
How much is this?
I'd like a piece of cake.
We don't have much time.
She has a lot of friends.
Would you like some coffee?

vocab.ex: I drink a lot of water.

levels.title: A2 · Básico
levels.description: Cuentas lo que pasó, comparas cosas, haces planes y das consejos sencillos.

units.title: ¿Dónde estabas?
units.subtitle: Pasado de to be: was / were
units.goal: Hablar de dónde estabas y cómo era algo en el pasado.

sections.heading: Was / were
sections.body:
- I / he / she / it → **was**
- you / we / they → **were**

> I was at home yesterday. They were tired.
> She **wasn't** at work. We **weren't** ready.
> **Were** you at the party? — Yes, I was. / No, I wasn't.

sections.heading: Expresiones de tiempo pasado
sections.body:
- **yesterday** (ayer), **yesterday morning**
- **last** night / week / month / year (la noche pasada, la semana pasada…)
- two days **ago** (hace dos días) — *ago* va **después** del tiempo
- **in** 2020 · **when** I was a child

> Where were you last night?
> I was born in 2004.  (nacer = **be born**)

examples.en: I was at home yesterday.
Where were you last night?
The movie was very good.
We weren't at the party.
Was it expensive?
I was born in Antigua.
They were in Guatemala two years ago.
examples.es: Estuvieron en Guatemala hace dos años.

examples.en: It was cold this morning.

vocab.ex: I was there two weeks ago.

exercises.prompt: The test ___ difficult. It was easy.
How ___ your weekend? — It was great!
___ you at work yesterday? — No, I wasn't.

units.title: Lo que hice
units.subtitle: Pasado simple: verbos regulares
units.goal: Contar lo que hiciste ayer o el fin de semana.

sections.heading: Forma afirmativa
sections.body:
Los verbos regulares agregan **-ed** (igual para todas las personas):

- work → work**ed**, play → play**ed**
- Terminados en e: + d → live → live**d**
- Consonante + y → **-ied**: study → stud**ied**
- Consonante-vocal-consonante corta: stop → sto**pped**, plan → pla**nned**

Pronunciación de -ed: /t/ worked, /d/ played, /ɪd/ want**ed**, need**ed** (solo después de t o d).

sections.heading: Negativo y preguntas con did
sections.body:
- Negativo: **didn't** + verbo base → *I didn't watch TV.*
- Pregunta: **Did** + sujeto + verbo base → *Did you call her?* — Yes, I did.
- Con palabra interrogativa: *What did you do yesterday?*

Después de did/didn't **nunca** va -ed: *Did you work?* (no *Did you worked?*)

examples.en: I worked until eight yesterday.
We played soccer on Sunday.
She studied all night.
Did you call your mom?
I didn't watch the game.
They visited their grandparents.
What did you do last weekend?
examples.es: ¿Qué hiciste el fin de semana pasado?

examples.en: The bus stopped suddenly.
examples.es: El bus se detuvo de repente.

vocab.ex: I tried sushi for the first time.

exercises.prompt: ___ she call you? — Yes, she did.

answers: I did not watch the game

units.title: Una historia
units.subtitle: Pasado simple: verbos irregulares
units.goal: Usar los verbos irregulares más comunes para contar historias.

sections.heading: Irregulares frecuentes
sections.body:
No siguen la regla del -ed; hay que memorizarlos:

- go → **went** · come → **came** · see → **saw**
- have → **had** · do → **did** · make → **made**
- get → **got** · take → **took** · give → **gave**
- eat → **ate** · drink → **drank** · buy → **bought**
- say → **said** · tell → **told** · think → **thought**
- find → **found** · leave → **left** · meet → **met**
- know → **knew** · write → **wrote** · read → **read** (se pronuncia "red")

En negativo y preguntas se usa **did + verbo base**: *I didn't go. Did you see it?*

sections.heading: Conectores para contar
sections.body:
**First**, … **Then**, … **After that**, … **Finally**, …

> First, we went to the market. Then we had lunch. After that, we took a tuk-tuk. Finally, we went home.

examples.en: We went to Lake Atitlán last month.
examples.es: Fuimos al lago de Atitlán el mes pasado.

units.title: Más grande, el mejor
units.subtitle: Comparativos y superlativos
units.goal: Comparar personas, lugares y cosas.

sections.heading: Comparativos
sections.body:
- Adjetivos cortos: + **-er than** → tall → tall**er than**, cheap → cheap**er than**
- Terminados en y: **-ier** → easy → eas**ier**, happy → happ**ier**
- Doble consonante: big → bi**gger**, hot → ho**tter**
- Adjetivos largos: **more … than** → **more expensive than**, **more interesting than**
- Irregulares: good → **better**, bad → **worse**, far → **farther/further**

Igualdad: **as … as** → *She's as tall as her brother.*

sections.heading: Superlativos
sections.body:
- Cortos: **the -est** → the tall**est**, the bigg**est**, the eas**iest**
- Largos: **the most** → the most beautiful
- Irregulares: **the best**, **the worst**

> It's the best restaurant **in** the city. (con lugares se usa **in**, no *of*)

examples.en: My brother is taller than me.
examples.es: Mi hermano es más alto que yo.

examples.en: This phone is cheaper than that one.
examples.es: Este teléfono es más barato que ese.

units.title: Planes y predicciones
units.subtitle: Futuro: going to y will
units.goal: Hablar de planes, decisiones del momento y predicciones.

sections.heading: Be going to
sections.body:
**am/is/are + going to + verbo**

- **Planes ya decididos**: *I'm going to visit my grandma on Sunday.*
- **Predicciones con evidencia**: *Look at those clouds. It's going to rain.*

> Are you going to study tonight? — Yes, I am.

sections.heading: Will
sections.body:
**will ('ll) + verbo** (igual para todas las personas). Negativo: **won't**.

- **Decisiones en el momento**: *The phone is ringing. I'll answer it.*
- **Promesas y ofrecimientos**: *I'll help you. I won't tell anyone.*
- **Predicciones / opiniones**: *I think it will be a great year.*

sections.heading: ¿Cuál uso?
sections.body:
Si ya lo **planeaste** antes → **going to**.
Si lo **decides ahora** u ofreces algo → **will**.

> A: We don't have milk. B: Really? **I'll** buy some. (decisión ahora)
> I'm **going to** buy milk after work. (plan)

units.title: Mi agenda
units.subtitle: Presente continuo para futuro, fechas y preposiciones de tiempo
units.goal: Hablar de citas y planes con fecha y hora.

sections.heading: Presente continuo con sentido futuro
sections.body:
Para **citas y planes ya organizados** (con hora, lugar o personas) se usa mucho el presente continuo:

> I'm meeting Ana at five.
> We're flying to Cancún on Friday.
> What are you doing this weekend?

sections.heading: In / on / at con tiempo
sections.body:
- **at** + hora exacta y momentos: at 7:00, at noon, at night, at the weekend (británico)
- **on** + días y fechas: on Monday, on May 5th, on my birthday, on the weekend (americano)
- **in** + meses, años, estaciones y partes del día: in March, in 2027, in the morning

Sin preposición con **this / next / last / every**: *next Monday*, *this week*.

sections.heading: Fechas
sections.body:
En inglés se usan **números ordinales**: first (1st), second (2nd), third (3rd), fourth (4th), fifth (5th)… twentieth (20th), twenty-first (21st).

> My birthday is on **May 5th** (se lee "May fifth").
> What's the date today? — It's **October 29th**.

units.title: ¿Alguna vez…?
units.subtitle: Introducción al present perfect
units.goal: Hablar de experiencias y de cosas recién hechas.

sections.heading: Forma
sections.body:
**have / has + participio pasado**

- Regulares: participio = -ed → work**ed**, visit**ed**
- Irregulares frecuentes: be → **been**, go → **gone/been**, see → **seen**, eat → **eaten**, do → **done**, make → **made**, have → **had**, write → **written**, take → **taken**

> I've (I have) visited Mexico. She's (she has) finished.
> I **haven't** seen it. **Have** you ever tried sushi?

sections.heading: Experiencias: ever / never
sections.body:
Para hablar de experiencias de la vida **sin decir cuándo**:

> **Have you ever** been to the US? — Yes, I have. / No, I haven't.
> I've **never** eaten sushi.

Si dices **cuándo** pasó, cambia a pasado simple: *I went there in 2023.*

sections.heading: Just / already / yet
sections.body:
- **just** = acabar de → *I've just arrived.* (acabo de llegar)
- **already** = ya (afirmativo) → *I've already eaten.*
- **yet** = ya (pregunta) / todavía (negativo), va al final → *Have you finished yet? I haven't finished yet.*

units.title: Deberías…
units.subtitle: Must, have to y should
units.goal: Hablar de obligaciones, reglas y dar consejos.

sections.heading: Have to / must
sections.body:
- **have to**: obligación (muy común en conversación). *I have to work tomorrow. She has to study.*
- **must**: obligación fuerte o regla, más formal o personal. *You must wear a seatbelt.*
- Pregunta: **Do you have to** work on Saturdays?

sections.heading: ¡Cuidado con el negativo!
sections.body:
- **don't have to** = no es necesario → *You don't have to come.* (puedes venir si quieres)
- **mustn't** = está prohibido → *You mustn't smoke here.*

Significan cosas muy distintas.

sections.heading: Should para consejos
sections.body:
**should / shouldn't + verbo** = deberías / no deberías:

> You should sleep more. You shouldn't drink so much coffee.
> What **should** I do?

Para opinar suave: *I think you should talk to her.*

units.title: Muy rápido, demasiado tarde
units.subtitle: Adverbios, too/enough y pronombres de objeto
units.goal: Describir cómo se hacen las cosas y decir si algo es suficiente.

sections.heading: Adverbios de modo
sections.body:
Dicen **cómo** se hace algo. Se forman con **-ly** (como el *-mente* del español):

- slow → slow**ly**, careful → careful**ly**, easy → eas**ily**
- Irregulares: good → **well**, fast → **fast**, hard → **hard**, late → **late**

> She speaks English **well**. (no *good*)
> He drives **carefully**.

sections.heading: Too y enough
sections.body:
- **too + adjetivo** = demasiado (problema) → *It's too expensive.*
- **adjetivo + enough** = suficientemente → *He isn't old enough to drive.*
- **enough + sustantivo** = suficiente → *We don't have enough time.*

sections.heading: Pronombres de objeto
sections.body:
Van **después** del verbo o preposición:

- I → **me** · you → **you** · he → **him** · she → **her**
- it → **it** · we → **us** · they → **them**

> Call **me** later. I love **them**. This is for **her**.

units.title: Mientras tanto…
units.subtitle: Pasado continuo y when / while
units.goal: Describir lo que estaba pasando cuando ocurrió algo.

sections.heading: Forma
sections.body:
**was / were + verbo -ing**

> I was sleeping at 11 p.m.
> They were playing when it started to rain.
> What **were** you doing? — I **was** working.

sections.heading: Pasado continuo + pasado simple
sections.body:
La acción **larga** (de fondo) va en continuo; la acción **corta** que la interrumpe, en simple:

> I **was cooking** when the phone **rang**.
> **While** we **were walking**, we **saw** an accident.

- **when** + acción corta (simple)
- **while** + acción larga (continuo)

units.title: Since and for
units.subtitle: Present perfect vs past simple
units.goal: Elegir bien entre present perfect y past simple, y usar for / since.

sections.heading: Unfinished time vs finished time
sections.body:
- **Past simple**: acción terminada en un momento **terminado** (yesterday, in 2020, last week, ago). *I lived in Xela in 2019.*
- **Present perfect**: conecta el pasado con **ahora** (resultado actual, experiencia, periodo que no ha terminado). *I've lived here for five years.* (todavía vivo aquí)

> I **lost** my keys yesterday. (historia terminada)
> I**'ve lost** my keys! (y ahora no las tengo)

sections.heading: For vs since
sections.body:
- **for** + duración → for two years, for a long time, for ages
- **since** + punto de inicio → since 2023, since Monday, since I was a child

> I've worked at BYTE **since** 2023. → I've worked there **for** almost three years.
> **How long have you** known her? (no *How long do you know her?*)

Error típico de hispanohablantes: *I live here since 2010* ❌ → **I've lived here since 2010** ✅

sections.heading: This week / today / this year
sections.body:
Si el periodo **no ha terminado**, se usa present perfect: *I've had three coffees today.*
Si ya terminó: *I had three coffees yesterday.*

units.title: I've been waiting

units.goal: Hablar de actividades que empezaron en el pasado y siguen (o acaban de terminar).

sections.heading: Simple vs continuous
sections.body:
- **Continuous**: énfasis en la **actividad** y su duración. *I've been painting the house.* (tal vez no terminé)
- **Simple**: énfasis en el **resultado** o la cantidad. *I've painted two rooms.* (terminadas)

También usamos el continuo para explicar **evidencia** de algo reciente:
> Your eyes are red. Have you been crying?

Recuerda: verbos de estado (know, like, want, be) normalmente no van en continuo → *I've known her for years.*

units.title: If it rains…
units.subtitle: First conditional y time clauses
units.goal: Hablar de situaciones posibles en el futuro y sus consecuencias.

sections.heading: First conditional
sections.body:
**If + present simple, will + verbo** → situaciones **reales o probables**:

> If it rains, we'll stay at home.
> If you don't study, you won't pass.
> What will you do if they offer you the job?

⚠️ Después de **if** NO se usa will: *If it will rain* ❌ → **If it rains** ✅

sections.heading: Unless, when, as soon as
sections.body:
Las mismas reglas aplican con:
- **unless** = if… not → *I won't go unless you come.* (no iré a menos que vengas)
- **when** → *I'll call you when I arrive.* (cuando llegue — en español subjuntivo, en inglés presente)
- **as soon as** (en cuanto), **before**, **after**, **until**

> I'll send it as soon as I finish.

units.title: If I were you
units.subtitle: Second conditional
units.goal: Imaginar situaciones irreales o poco probables y dar consejos.

sections.heading: Form
sections.body:
**If + past simple, would + verbo** → situaciones **imaginarias**, poco probables o irreales en el presente/futuro:

> If I had more time, I would learn French.
> If I won the lottery, I'd buy a house for my parents.
> What would you do if you lost your phone?

El pasado aquí **no** habla del pasado: habla de algo hipotético.

sections.heading: If I were you…
sections.body:
Con to be se usa **were** para todas las personas (especialmente en inglés formal):

> If I **were** you, I'd accept the offer. (yo que tú…)
> If she **were** here, she'd know what to do.

En conversación también se escucha *If I was…*, pero **If I were you** es la expresión fija para dar consejos.

sections.heading: 1st vs 2nd conditional

- *If I **get** the job, I**'ll** move.* → es posible, lo veo real.
- *If I **got** the job, I**'d** move.* → lo veo poco probable o lo estoy imaginando.

units.title: It was built in…

sections.heading: Form
sections.body:
**be + participio pasado**

- Presente: *English **is spoken** all over the world.*
- Pasado: *Tikal **was built** by the Maya.*
- Con agente (opcional): **by** + persona → *The app was designed **by** a student.*

Negativo y preguntas: *It wasn't made in China. Where was it made?*

sections.heading: When do we use it?
sections.body:
- Cuando **no sabemos** o **no importa** quién hizo la acción: *My phone was stolen.*
- Para **procesos** y textos formales: *The data is stored in the cloud.*
- Para enfocar el objeto: *This song was written in 1985.*

En español a veces usamos "se": *Se habla inglés* → **English is spoken**.

units.goal: Unir ideas y describir personas, cosas y lugares con who, which, that y where.

sections.heading: Relative pronouns
sections.body:
- **who** → personas: *The woman **who** lives next door is a doctor.*
- **which** → cosas: *The laptop **which** I bought is fast.*
- **that** → personas o cosas (muy común en conversación)
- **where** → lugares: *That's the café **where** we met.*
- **whose** → posesión: *He's the guy **whose** car was stolen.*

sections.heading: Omitting the pronoun
sections.body:
Si el pronombre es el **objeto** del verbo, se puede omitir:

> The movie (that) **we watched** was great. ✅
> The man **who called** you is here. → aquí *who* es sujeto, no se omite.

⚠️ No repitas el pronombre: *The book that I read **it*** ❌ → *The book that I read* ✅

sections.heading: Backshift
sections.body:
Cuando reportamos con **said** o **told**, el tiempo verbal normalmente "retrocede":

- present → past: "I **am** tired." → She said she **was** tired.
- present continuous → past continuous
- past / present perfect → past perfect: "I **saw** it." → He said he **had seen** it.
- will → **would**; can → **could**

También cambian pronombres y referencias: *now → then*, *today → that day*, *tomorrow → the next day*, *here → there*.

sections.heading: Say vs tell
sections.body:
- **say** (something): *She **said** (that) she was busy.*
- **tell** + persona: *She **told me** (that) she was busy.*

❌ *She said me* → ✅ *She told me* / *She said to me*

sections.heading: Verb + -ing
sections.body:
Después de algunos verbos va **-ing**:

**enjoy, mind, finish, avoid, suggest, keep, practice, miss, consider, can't stand**

> I enjoy **reading**. Do you mind **waiting**? I've finished **working**.

También después de **preposiciones**: *I'm good **at** cooking. Thanks **for** helping. I'm interested **in** learning.*
Y como sujeto: ***Learning** English is fun.*

sections.heading: Verb + to-infinitive
sections.body:
Después de otros va **to + verbo**:

**want, need, decide, hope, plan, learn, promise, agree, refuse, would like, afford**

> I want **to travel**. She decided **to quit**. I'd like **to order**, please.

sections.heading: Change of meaning
sections.body:
- **stop -ing** = dejar de · **stop to** = detenerse para → *I stopped smoking.* / *I stopped to buy water.*
- **remember -ing** = recordar algo pasado · **remember to** = acordarse de hacer → *Remember to call her!*
- **try -ing** = probar · **try to** = intentar

units.title: By the time I arrived…
units.subtitle: Narrative tenses: past perfect (simple & continuous)
units.goal: Tell stories clearly, showing what happened first.

sections.heading: Past perfect simple
sections.body:
**had + past participle** → an action that happened **before** another past action.

> When I got to the station, the train **had** already **left**.
> She was nervous because she **hadn't flown** before.

Without it, the order changes: *When I arrived, the train left* = it left when I arrived.

🇪🇸 Equivale a "había + participio": *ya se había ido*.

sections.heading: Past perfect continuous
sections.body:
**had been + -ing** → a longer activity that continued up to a point in the past.

> I **had been waiting** for an hour when she finally called.
> His eyes were red because he **had been crying**.

sections.heading: Narrative tenses together
sections.body:
- **Past simple**: main events → *I opened the door.*
- **Past continuous**: background → *It was raining.*
- **Past perfect**: earlier events → *Someone had broken the window.*

units.title: If I had known…
units.subtitle: Third and mixed conditionals
units.goal: Talk about imaginary past situations and regrets.

sections.heading: Third conditional
sections.body:
**If + past perfect, would have + past participle** → an imaginary **past** (it didn't happen).

> If I **had studied**, I **would have passed**. (I didn't study, I didn't pass.)
> If you **had told** me, I **could have helped**.
> We **wouldn't have got** lost if we **had taken** the map.

🇪🇸 *Si hubiera estudiado, habría aprobado.*

sections.heading: Mixed conditionals
sections.body:
Mixing times:

- Past condition → present result: *If I **had taken** that job, I **would be** rich now.*
- Present condition → past result: *If I **were** more organized, I **wouldn't have missed** the deadline.*

sections.heading: Pronunciation
sections.body:
In speech, **would have** sounds like *would've* /ˈwʊdəv/; **had** becomes *'d*:
*If I'd known, I would've come.*
Never write *would of* — it's a common mistake even for native speakers.

sections.heading: Passive in all tenses
sections.body:
- Present continuous: *The road **is being repaired**.*
- Present perfect: *The results **have been published**.*
- Future / modals: *It **will be done** tomorrow. It **must be signed**.*
- Infinitive / gerund: *I want **to be told**. I hate **being interrupted**.*

sections.heading: Have / get something done
sections.body:
When someone else does something **for you** (usually a service):

> I **had my car fixed**. (A mechanic fixed it.)
> She's **getting her hair cut** tomorrow.
> We **had our house painted** last year.

🇪🇸 *Me cortaron el pelo* → **I had my hair cut** (not *I cut my hair*, which means you did it yourself).

sections.heading: It is said that…

Reporting passive (news, formal):

> **It is said that** the hotel is haunted. → The hotel **is said to be** haunted.
> **It is believed that** he left the country. → He **is believed to have left** the country.

sections.heading: Reported questions
sections.body:
Use **normal word order** (no inversion, no do/did):

> "Where **do you** live?" → She asked me where **I lived**.
> "**Did you** see it?" → He asked **if/whether** I had seen it.

sections.heading: Reporting verbs
sections.body:
Instead of always using *said*, use more precise verbs:

- **verb + to-infinitive**: agree, offer, promise, refuse, threaten → *He **offered to drive** me home.*
- **verb + someone + to-infinitive**: ask, tell, advise, remind, warn, persuade → *She **reminded me to call** my mom.*
- **verb + -ing**: admit, deny, suggest, recommend → *He **denied taking** the money.*
- **verb + preposition + -ing**: apologize for, insist on, accuse someone of → *She **apologized for being** late.*

sections.heading: Criticism and regret

- **should have / ought to have + p.p.** → it was a good idea but you didn't do it → *You **should have told** me.*
- **shouldn't have + p.p.** → you did it but it was a bad idea → *I **shouldn't have eaten** so much.*

sections.heading: Deduction about the past
sections.body:
- **must have + p.p.** → I'm sure it happened → *She **must have forgotten**.*
- **might / may / could have + p.p.** → maybe it happened → *He **might have missed** the bus.*
- **can't / couldn't have + p.p.** → I'm sure it didn't happen → *They **can't have finished** already.*

sections.heading: Past possibility
sections.body:
- **could have + p.p.** → it was possible but didn't happen → *You **could have died**!*
- **needn't have + p.p.** / **didn't need to** → *You **needn't have brought** a gift.* (you did, but it wasn't necessary)

sections.body:
- **although / even though** + clause → *Although it was raining, we went out.*
- **despite / in spite of** + noun or **-ing** → *Despite the rain, we went out. / Despite **being** tired, she kept working.*
- **however** → starts a new sentence, followed by a comma → *It was expensive. **However**, it was worth it.*
- **whereas / while** → compares two facts → *I love coffee, **whereas** my sister prefers tea.*

❌ *Despite it was raining* → ✅ *Despite the rain* / *Despite the fact that it was raining*

sections.heading: Cause, result, addition
sections.body:
- Cause: **because** + clause, **because of / due to** + noun
- Result: **so**, **therefore**, **as a result**
- Addition: **moreover**, **furthermore**, **in addition**, **besides**
- Purpose: **so that**, **in order to**

> The flight was canceled **due to** bad weather. **As a result**, we stayed another night.

units.title: Which, by the way, …
units.subtitle: Non-defining relative clauses and participle clauses
units.goal: Add extra information elegantly and make sentences more concise.

sections.heading: Non-defining relative clauses
sections.body:
They add **extra** information. Use **commas**, and **never** use *that*:

> My brother, **who lives in Colombia**, is an engineer.
> Antigua, **which** was the capital, is a UNESCO site.

**which** can refer to the whole previous idea:
> He didn't call, **which** was strange.

sections.heading: Participle clauses
sections.body:
Shorter, more advanced way to combine sentences:

- **-ing** (active): *The man **sitting** next to me was snoring.* (who was sitting)
- **past participle** (passive): *The app, **developed** in Guatemala, has 1M users.*
- Time/reason: ***Having finished** the report, I went home.* (After I had finished…)
- ***Not knowing** what to do, she called me.*

units.title: Make or do?

sections.heading: Make vs do
sections.body:
- **make**: create or produce → make a mistake, make a decision, make money, make friends, make progress, make a phone call
- **do**: tasks and activities → do homework, do the dishes, do business, do a favor, do your best, do research

🇪🇸 *Hacer* is both, so you have to learn the collocations.

sections.heading: Common phrasal verbs
sections.body:
- **figure out** = understand / solve · **come up with** = think of (an idea)
- **run out of** = have no more · **put off** = postpone
- **get along with** = have a good relationship · **look into** = investigate
- **turn down** = reject · **carry on** = continue · **give up** = stop trying

sections.heading: Word formation
sections.body:
- Nouns: -tion (decide → decision), -ment (develop → development), -ness (happy → happiness), -ity (possible → possibility)
- Adjectives: -ful (use → useful), -less (use → useless), -able (afford → affordable), -ive (create → creative)
- Negative prefixes: **un**likely, **im**possible, **in**credible, **dis**agree, **ir**responsible

units.title: Never have I seen…
units.subtitle: Inversion for emphasis
units.goal: Use inversion to sound emphatic and formal.

sections.heading: Negative adverbials + inversion
sections.body:
When a sentence starts with a negative or restrictive expression, the auxiliary comes **before** the subject (like a question):

- **Never** have I seen such a mess.
- **Rarely / Seldom** do we get a chance like this.
- **Not only** did she win, **but** she also broke the record.
- **No sooner** had I arrived **than** it started to rain.
- **Hardly / Scarcely** had we sat down **when** the phone rang.
- **Under no circumstances** should you share your password.
- **Only then / Only when / Only after** … did I understand.
- **Little** did he know that…

sections.heading: When to use it
sections.body:
Inversion is typical of **formal writing, speeches and storytelling**. In everyday conversation it can sound dramatic — which is sometimes exactly the effect you want.

Neutral: *I had never seen anything like it.*
Emphatic: ***Never had I seen** anything like it.*

sections.heading: It-clefts
sections.body:
**It is/was + focus + that/who…** → highlights one element:

- ***It was the window that** Ana broke.* (not the door)

**What + clause + be + focus** → builds suspense and emphasis:

> **What we did was** (to) call the police.
> **All I want is** some peace and quiet.
> **The reason (why) I called is that** I need your help.

sections.heading: Inverted conditionals
sections.body:
In formal English, *if* can be dropped and the auxiliary inverted:

- ***Should** you need help, call me.* = If you should need help…
- ***Were** I in your position, I would resign.* = If I were…
- ***Had** I known, I would have come.* = If I had known…

sections.heading: Alternatives to if
sections.body:
- **provided / providing (that)**, **as long as**, **on condition that** → *You can borrow it **as long as** you return it.*
- **suppose / supposing / what if** → ***Supposing** you lost your job, what would you do?*
- **otherwise** → *Hurry up, **otherwise** we'll be late.*
- **but for / if it weren't for / if it hadn't been for** → ***But for** your help, I would have failed.*
- **were to** (hypothetical future) → *If the company **were to** close, many people would lose their jobs.*

units.title: It would appear that…
units.subtitle: Hedging and softening
units.goal: Express opinions cautiously and diplomatically, especially in academic and professional contexts.

sections.heading: Why hedge?
sections.body:
In academic writing, meetings and emails, strong statements can sound arrogant or inaccurate. **Hedging** shows caution and politeness.

- Strong: *This method is better.*
- Hedged: *This method **appears to be** somewhat more effective.*

sections.heading: Tools for hedging
sections.body:
- Verbs: **seem, appear, tend to, suggest, indicate** → *The data **suggests** that…*
- Modals: **may, might, could, would** → *This **could** be due to…*
- Adverbs: **possibly, arguably, apparently, relatively, to some extent**
- Phrases: ***It would appear that…***, ***There is some evidence that…***, ***It is likely that…***
- Softeners in speech: ***I'm not sure, but…***, ***I'd say…***, ***Correct me if I'm wrong, but…***, ***I was wondering if…***

units.subtitle: Nominalisation and formal register
units.goal: Write in a formal, academic or professional style.

sections.heading: Nominalisation
sections.body:
Formal English often turns **verbs and adjectives into nouns**, making text more objective and dense:

- *We **analyzed** the data and **discovered** that…* → *An **analysis** of the data led to the **discovery** that…*
- *Because prices **increased** quickly…* → *Due to the rapid **increase** in prices…*
- *If the team **is not available**…* → *In the event of the team's **unavailability**…*

sections.heading: Formal vs informal vocabulary
sections.body:
- get → **obtain / receive** · buy → **purchase** · ask for → **request**
- help → **assist** · need → **require** · start → **commence / initiate**
- find out → **discover / ascertain** · enough → **sufficient** · about → **approximately**
- but → **however / nevertheless** · so → **therefore / consequently**

Avoid contractions, phrasal verbs and vague words (*things, stuff, a lot of*) in formal writing.

units.goal: Express degrees of certainty with precision.

sections.heading: Certainty scale
sections.body:
- **bound to / sure to / certain to** → almost certain → *It's **bound to** rain; it always does in October.*
- **(highly) likely to / the chances are (that)** → probable → *She's **likely to** get the promotion.*
- **may well / could well** → quite possible → *Prices **may well** rise again.*
- **unlikely to / there's little chance of** → improbable → *He's **unlikely to** agree.*
- **there's no way** (informal) → impossible → ***There's no way** we'll finish today.*

sections.heading: Useful nouns and adjectives
sections.body:
- **a good chance / a slim chance**: *There's a slim chance we'll win.*
- **in all likelihood** = very probably
- **odds**: *The odds are against us.*
- **inevitable**, **doubtful**, **conceivable**

- **so / not** replace a clause: *Is it going to rain? — I think **so**. / I hope **not**.* (also: I suppose so, I'm afraid not, I guess so)
- **one / ones** replace countable nouns: *I don't like this shirt; I prefer the blue **one**.*
- **do so** (formal) replaces a verb phrase: *He promised to call, but he didn't **do so**.*

sections.heading: Ellipsis
sections.body:
Leave out words that are obvious from context:

- *I wanted to go, but I couldn't (go).*
- *She can speak French and so **can** I.* / *I'm not tired and neither **is** she.*
- *"Have you finished?" "Not yet (finished)."*
- *I'd love **to** (come).* — keep **to**.
- *"Are you coming?" "I might (come)."*

units.title: Let's get the ball rolling
units.subtitle: Idioms and fixed expressions for discussion
units.goal: Use idiomatic language naturally in meetings and conversations.

sections.heading: At work and in meetings
sections.body:
- **get the ball rolling** = start something
- **be on the same page** = agree / understand the same thing
- **touch base** = make brief contact
- **think outside the box** = think creatively
- **cut corners** = do something badly to save time/money
- **back to square one** = start again from the beginning
- **a win-win situation** = good for everyone

sections.heading: In conversation
sections.body:
- **it's not my cup of tea** = I don't really like it
- **hit the nail on the head** = describe exactly right
- **beat around the bush** = avoid the main topic
- **a piece of cake** = very easy
- **take it with a grain of salt** = don't believe it completely
- **once in a blue moon** = very rarely
- **the elephant in the room** = an obvious problem nobody mentions

Use idioms sparingly — too many sound unnatural.

units.title: I was wondering…
units.subtitle: Tense for distance and nuance
units.goal: Use tenses not for time, but for politeness, distance and attitude.

sections.heading: Distancing with past forms
sections.body:
Past and continuous forms make requests and statements **less direct**:

- *Do you want…?* → ***Did you want** anything else?* (waiter, polite)
- *I hope you can help* → ***I was hoping** you could help.*
- *I wonder if…* → ***I was wondering** if…*
- ***I wanted to ask** you something.* (but I'm asking now)

sections.heading: Would for habits and 'was going to'
sections.body:
- **would** for repeated past actions (storytelling, nostalgic): *Every summer, we **would** go to the lake.* (not with states: *I would have a dog* ❌)
- **was / were going to** → a plan that didn't happen: *I **was going to** call you, but I fell asleep.*
- **will** for typical behavior / annoyance: *She **will** keep talking during movies!*
- **be always -ing** for irritating habits: *He's **always losing** his keys.*

units.title: Be that as it may

sections.heading: Concession and contrast
sections.body:
- **Be that as it may** = even so → *The plan is risky. **Be that as it may**, it's our best option.*
- **Granted, … (but)** → ***Granted**, it's expensive, but it'll last for years.*
- **Admittedly** → ***Admittedly**, I didn't read the whole report.*
- **Notwithstanding** (formal) = despite
- **Even so / All the same / Nonetheless**

sections.heading: Structuring an argument
sections.body:
- Adding: **What is more**, **Not to mention**, **Coupled with**
- Clarifying: **That is to say**, **In other words**, **To put it another way**
- Focusing: **As far as … is concerned**, **With regard to**, **In terms of**
- Concluding: **All things considered**, **On balance**, **In the final analysis**
- Changing topic: **Incidentally**, **By the way**, **Speaking of which**

units.title: Mind your register
units.subtitle: Register shifting: formal, neutral, informal
units.goal: Rewrite the same message for different audiences.

sections.heading: Same idea, three registers
sections.body:
- Informal: *Sorry, can't make it tonight — something came up.*
- Neutral: *I'm sorry, but I won't be able to come tonight. Something has come up.*
- Formal: *Please accept my apologies; I regret that I will be unable to attend this evening due to unforeseen circumstances.*

sections.heading: Markers of register
sections.body:
**Informal**: contractions, phrasal verbs, ellipsis (*Sounds good!*), slang (*gonna, kinda*), direct questions.
**Formal**: full forms, Latin-based vocabulary (*commence, endeavour*), passive voice, impersonal structures (*It is advisable to…*), indirect questions (*Could you tell me whether…*).

Common pitfall for advanced learners: being **too formal** in casual contexts (sounds cold or sarcastic) — e.g., Slack messages to a colleague don't need *I hereby inform you*.

units.title: Rarely seen, much admired
units.subtitle: Fronting and emphatic structures
units.goal: Move elements to the front and use emphatic forms for style and impact.

sections.heading: Fronting
sections.body:
Placing an element at the start for emphasis or contrast:

- *I can't stand his attitude* → ***His attitude** I can't stand.*
- ***Strange** as it may seem, I enjoyed it.* (= Although it may seem strange)
- ***Try as I might**, I couldn't open it.* (= However hard I tried)
- ***Much as** I admire her, I disagree.* (= Although I admire her a lot)
- ***Down came** the rain.* / ***Here comes** the bus.* (locative inversion)

sections.heading: Emphatic do and intensifiers
sections.body:
- Emphatic **do/does/did**: *I **do** understand your concerns. She **did** call — you just missed it.*
- **the very**: *That's **the very** thing I was looking for.*
- **whatsoever / at all**: *I have no idea **whatsoever**.*
- **on earth / ever** in questions: *What **on earth** happened? Who **ever** told you that?*

units.title: Slim, skinny or slender?
units.subtitle: Connotation and near-synonyms
units.goal: Choose words with the right shade of meaning.

sections.heading: Positive, neutral, negative
sections.body:
Words can mean almost the same thing but carry different **connotations**:

- **slender / slim** (positive) · **thin** (neutral) · **skinny / scrawny** (negative)
- **confident** (+) · **self-assured** (+/neutral) · **arrogant / cocky** (−)
- **thrifty / economical** (+) · **careful with money** (neutral) · **stingy / cheap** (−)
- **curious** (+) · **inquisitive** (neutral) · **nosy** (−)
- **determined** (+) · **stubborn** (−) · **pig-headed** (very −)

sections.heading: Precise verbs
sections.body:
Advanced speakers prefer precise verbs over *say / look / walk + adverb*:

- say → **whisper, mutter, claim, insist, point out, hint**
- look → **glance** (quick), **stare** (long), **glare** (angry), **peer** (difficult to see)
- walk → **stroll** (relaxed), **stride** (confident), **wander** (no direction), **limp** (injured)
- increase → **soar** (rapidly), **creep up** (slowly), **double**

units.title: Food for thought
units.subtitle: Figurative and idiomatic language
units.goal: Understand and use metaphor, understatement and irony.

sections.heading: Metaphor in everyday English
sections.body:
Many abstract ideas are expressed through concrete images:

- Ideas are food: *food for thought*, *half-baked idea*, *digest the information*, *hard to swallow*
- Time is money: *spend / waste / save / invest time*, *running out of time*
- Argument is war: *defend a position*, *attack a point*, *shoot down an idea*
- Understanding is seeing: *I see what you mean*, *shed light on*, *a clear explanation*

sections.heading: Understatement and irony
sections.body:
British and American speakers often use **understatement**: *It's **not exactly** cheap* (= very expensive). *I'm **not the biggest fan** of…* (= I dislike).

Irony: saying the opposite with a specific tone: *Oh, **great**. Another meeting.*

Recognizing these is key at C2: the literal meaning isn't the real message.
